21279-2-b-r-0-2-b:
Kurt Vonnegut Jr. published this short story in Worlds of If in January 1962, taking its title from Hamlet's question, spelled out in digits and letters. Everything is perfectly swell in its future: no prisons, slums, poverty, or wars. All diseases are conquered, and so is old age.

Death, barring accidents, is an adventure for volunteers, and America's population is held at forty million. In a Chicago lying-in hospital, Edward K. Wehling Jr., fifty-six and young by the age's standards, waits for his wife to bear triplets. In this world, new life requires room. The title gives the way out, and the story turns on who must take it.
22037-the-life-public-services-and-selec:
Rutherford B. Hayes rose from Civil War general to Governor of Ohio and then President. Campaign lives like this one introduced such a candidate to the voters. The book traces the Hayes line back to George Hayes of Scotland, who settled at Windsor, Connecticut, in 1682. From that stock, it argues, came a fitting Republican candidate for President.

Family history gives way to war service, Congress, and the governorship. A generous share of the volume prints Hayes's own speeches, so readers could judge his words directly. Such books were tools of persuasion as much as records. This one preserves the image of Hayes that his party carried into the disputed election of 1876.

doe-osti-3365798-implementation-of-a-hig: At many times the speed of sound, air hugs a vehicle's skin in a thin, hot boundary layer. Jonathan Murray implemented a math method that predicts that layer's behavior for any smooth body shape at high Mach numbers. The tool helps designers of hypersonic craft and missiles work faster.
doe-osti-3484473-radiolytic-gas-generati: Mo-99 got gas-generated, and this DOE text covers radiolytic pressure buildup. The pages detail the generation findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The system was closed. The data were nuclear. The Mo-99 were buildup. The closed were system.
govdocs-archive_org-jfk-assassination-re:
In 2025 the United States government released a new wave of records on the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, under laws requiring the remaining files to come out. Batch two of that release gathers the documents as they were issued.

The papers run to memos, cables, and reports from the agencies that held Kennedy-era files, many of them previously redacted or withheld. Researchers read such batches slowly, comparing versions against earlier releases to find what changed. The file preserves the batch as a public record, complete as issued, for exactly that work.
govdocs-archive_org-national-socialist-a:
The National Socialist Anthology collects writings on the history and works of Heinrich Himmler and certain members of the SS. Its dedication is to Himmler himself, as Reichsführer-SS, which tells the reader plainly where the volume stands.

The anthology presents Nazi material in the movement's own terms, as a record of what its adherents wrote and honored. One technical caution: this copy's text layer is scrambled by a character-substitution cipher, which limits searching and reading on screen. It is presented as an archive holding, without endorsement, for historians of the period.
govdocs-archive_org-perspectives-on-init:
René Guénon published Perspectives on Initiation in 1946, near the end of his life. Guénon founded the Traditionalist school, which held that real spiritual teaching passes through unbroken chains of initiation.

The book explains what initiation is and is not: the rites that confer it, the signs by which it is known, and the slow waking of the soul it begins. Guénon separates true initiation from clubs and ceremonies that merely copy its form. For his school, the volume is a key statement of how a seeker actually enters a tradition.
govdocs-archive_org-russian-racial-scien: Russian Racial Science, Volume 2: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-stepan-bandera-selec: Stepan Bandera: Selected Works, Volume 1 - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-analects-of-conf:
The Analects gathers the sayings of Confucius and his talks with students, recorded by his followers after his death in 479 BC. Presented here in English, the text comes with a learned word-list keyed to book and verse for close study.

Short exchanges carry the teaching: respect for parents, care in speech, rule by moral example rather than force, and learning as a lifelong duty. Those ideas ordered Chinese family life, education, and government for two thousand years. The Analects remains the base of Confucius's school of thought, and this edition's word-list helps readers follow key terms as they recur across the whole work.
govdocs-archive_org-the-presocratic-phil: The Presocratic Philosophers gathers the earliest Greek thinkers into one volume. It runs from the forerunners who first tried to explain the world's making through to the Sophists of Athens. Thinkers like Heraclitus and Parmenides left only fragments, quoted by later writers. A collection like this one sets those fragments in order so readers can follow the birth of philosophy itself, from water and fire to atoms and argument.
govdocs-archive_org-the-symbolism-of-fre: Freemasonic Symbolism presents Freemasonry as an initiatory institution whose real teaching stays hidden in plain sight. The exposition explains the fraternity's symbols as carriers of that teaching. Masonic signs, tools, and temple forms have drawn curious readers for three centuries. A guide like this one walks through them as a system rather than a code to crack. It serves readers of fraternal history and of the symbolic reading of ritual.
govdocs-archive_org-time-machines-norber: Norbert Jürgen Ratthofer wrote Time Machines about devices classed as stationary and non-stationary. The topic belongs to fringe science: claims that time itself can be engineered. The library holds the work as an archive item, without backing. It serves readers who collect speculative writing on time travel, where physics terms and secret-project stories tend to mix. The volume presents its claims in full for that audience.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-b:
Part B continues David Hume's History of England in the 1860 Virtue edition, three volumes split into six parts. Hume published the history from 1754 to 1762, working backward from the Stuarts to Caesar. His aim was a full national story told with a steady, skeptical mind.

The chapters in each part march year by year through reigns, wars, and parliaments. Hume treats heroes and villains with the same level gaze, which shocked readers used to party histories. The set holds all seventy-one chapters of the complete work. Part B keeps the narrative rolling in the prose that made Hume the most read historian of his century.
jeremy-and-hamlet-a-chronicle-of-certain: Jeremy and Hamlet, a chronicle of certain incidents in the lives of a boy, a dog, by Hugh Walpole. The boy and his dog. This book preserves that novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
lincoln-s-gettysburg-address-given-novem:
Abraham Lincoln delivered this address at Gettysburg on November 19, 1863. The battlefield near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, had become a cemetery ground. Project Gutenberg first issued the text among its earliest etexts. This retranscription was officially re-released on November 19, 1993.

Lincoln opens four score and seven years before his speech. He says the brave men there consecrated the ground already. The living, he argues, must dedicate themselves to unfinished work. The short speech remains America's most famous act of public mourning. The address runs only a few hundred words in full. Gutenberg timed this re-release for the speech's 130th anniversary.
the-cruise-of-the-jasper-b: Don Marquis's comic novel about a meek clerk who buys a ship sight unseen and sails into a series of romantic misadventures. Mistaken identities, runaway heiresses, and high-seas farce pile up in the author's breezy, wisecracking style. Published in 1916, it is light entertainment by the creator of Archy the cockroach, written purely for laughs.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1602-b:
A companion gathering from Zetzner's Strasbourg press in 1602 adds more tracts to the Theatrum Chemicum. Lazarus Zetzner kept collecting the chief writers on alchemy in Latin. Together with the first gathering, it helped form one shared canon for the art.

More treatises on the great work fill these pages, in the same grand format. Readers meet famed adepts, their symbols, their furnaces, and their claims. The set gave scattered texts a stable home in print. Anyone who owned both printings held the core library of early modern alchemy, the books that serious students reached for first.
types-of-children-s-literature-a-collect: Educator Walter Barnes assembled this landmark anthology showing the many kinds of writing for children — fairy tales, fables, myths, poetry, and realistic stories. Each section is chosen to show teachers and parents what children's literature could be at its best. Long used in classrooms, it helped establish the serious study of books for young readers.
un-ga-res-49-236-b:
Native peoples won a named place in Guatemala's peace under a deal marked in Resolution 49/236 B. On 31 March 1995, the state and the rebel URNG signed the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The vote recalls the chain of texts that set up the UN rights mission in Guatemala in 1994, and stretched its term by six months that March.

The mission chief's second report lies before the Assembly. Its counsel, sent to both the state and the URNG, weighs how each kept its pledges under the rights deal. The text takes note of that counsel in full. The native deal, with the rights mission to check it, formed one pillar of the peace that ended the war in 1996.
un-ga-res-51-198-b:
Guatemala's peace deals needed a UN watch, and Resolution 51/198 B keeps that watch in place. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994. In December 1996, the government and the rebel URNG signed a firm and lasting peace at Guatemala City. The vote stretches the mission's mandate for one year, to 31 March 1998, in a fresh form fit for peace.

The text recalls the chain of votes that built the mission, from 1990 on. The Secretary-General was asked to counsel how the mission's shape and staff should change for its new task. That task: check that the pledges of the peace, on rights and far more, were kept in daily life.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 49/236 B, adopted on 14 September 1995, renewed the Guatemala human rights verification mission for six months, until 18 March 1996. The Assembly stressed the weight of the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples, signed by the parties on 31 March 1995. It called it a landmark in the International Decade of the World's Indigenous People.

The parties were told to carry out the mission director's advice from his first and second reports. They were told to keep their human rights promises, now including the indigenous peoples agreement's rights parts. The text also urges agreement on land and economic questions, the next item in the talks, toward an early final peace.

General Assembly Resolution 51/198 B, adopted on 27 March 1997, reshaped the United Nations presence in Guatemala after peace. The final peace accord of 29 December 1996 had ended the long internal conflict. Work was under way on checking the ceasefire, pulling forces apart, and disarming and demobilizing fighters. Military observers attached to the mission watched that work.

The Assembly renamed the human rights mission the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala. It renewed it for one year, until 31 March 1998, to verify all the peace accords. Both parties were praised for their steady search for peace and called on to keep every promise they had made.
william-harvey-and-the-discovery-of-the-: Thomas Henry Huxley on William Harvey and the circulation of the blood: the great discovery retold. The father of physiology, honored by Darwin's bulldog. Medical history. Harvey's heart pumps through Huxley's prose, the great discovery, nobly told.
